items.content:
RT @0xpwnie: This just reminded me of a happening i heard of back when i was in junior school: The Night Shot Flaw aka see-through camcorders

Sony’s consumer Handycam camcorders (models like the CCD-TRV65 and others with the NightShot/NightShot infrared mode) could record in very low light or darkness by mechanically moving aside the normal IR-cut filter and using near-infrared sensitivity (plus built-in IR LEDs for illumination). The mode produced the familiar greenish monochrome image.

Under very specific daytime conditions; bright sunlight (which contains a lot of near-IR), certain thin/dark or loosely woven fabrics (especially some swimsuits, black synthetics, or sheer materials), often with an added visible-light-blocking IR-pass filter over the lens, and the right angles/distance, the clothing could appear partially translucent in the IR image. This revealed body silhouettes or underwear outlines rather than true X-ray detail or full nudity. It worked because some fabrics absorb/reflect visible light differently from near-IR wavelengths.

A Japanese men’s magazine highlighted the effect, it spread quickly, and Sony confirmed limited reproducibility under those constrained conditions. They halted further shipments of the affected models, modified the feature (so NightShot would not engage in sufficient ambient light on later units), and did not issue a full recall of the hundreds of thousands already sold. Demand for the unmodified cameras spiked briefly because of the publicity.

It was never reliable “X-ray vision,” required ideal lighting/fabrics/setup, and was more of an unintended side effect of the IR sensitivity than a designed flaw. Similar IR transparency effects can still appear with certain modern night-vision or modified cameras under the right conditions, which is why some athletic wear (e.g., for the Olympics) has been developed with IR-blocking properties.

RT @snehalantani: Attackers don't "hack in" with CVE's or zero days, they log in with credentials they've compromised. As security practitioners this isn't news, however given the vulnpocolypse craze and maniacal focus on squashing application bugs, it's a principle that's important for all to remember.... and here's a clear example from a real customer environment...

our AI Hacker NodeZero was run against a large enterprise. No humans in or on the loop, no prior knowledge of the environment, just point+click+hack

During that pentest (or, "agentic attacker swarm" is what the cool kids are calling it now  🤣 ), NodeZero methodically compromised credentials using a variety of techniques.

In this case, NodeZero:

- successfully cracked 61k+ credentials due to weak passwords

- and it took ~5 mins of GPU time to crack a single credential

- A single credential provided access to 11k hosts (!!) due to credential reuse

- 1300+ credentials were compromised because the EDR on the host wasn't configured properly (happens all the time)

- 1200+ credentials had easily guessed passwords

This is the attacker's perspective... so while organizations surge resources into fixing vulnerabilities in custom code, remember the attackers have a vote... and it's much easier for attackers to reuse credential compromise techniques across thousands of targets versus spending a ton of time researching a zero day in your custom app that cannot be reused elsewhere

items.content:
Always great to hear old friends sharing their insights on a podcast. Even better when they mention my name! Really appreciate it.🙏

Let me add my two cents on `TraderTraitor` from my personal perspective. @craiu, you might remember `AppleJeus`, one of the earliest Lazarus campaigns targeting macOS users that we discovered back in 2018. Around that time, we started seeing Lazarus-associated activities emerge as several distinct clusters. `AppleJeus` was one of the campaigns we investigated, and the attackers continued using similar tactics,  trojanized cryptocurrency trading applications, over the following years. 

In 2022, CISA introduced the `TraderTraitor` name for a series of malicious cryptocurrency applications that shared similarities with earlier AppleJeus operations. Since then, `TraderTraitor` has become a widely used name, while different security vendors have tracked overlapping activities under names such as Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Slow Pisces, and Pressure Chollima.

Honestly, I lost visibility into some of this group's activities for a while. However, they never stopped targeting the cryptocurrency industry. Their operations evolved to include fake recruitment, malicious take-home coding assessments, and trojanized developer tools involving npm, PyPI, Ruby, and other ecosystems, contributing to several major cryptocurrency thefts.

One case that particularly caught my attention was the KelpDAO incident, documented in LayerZero's investigation report: https://t.co/T7IbKEK26L

The malware infection chain itself was interesting, but the post-exploitation activities were what really stood out to me. The attackers demonstrated a clear understanding of cloud infrastructure, internal workflows, and how cryptocurrency businesses operate behind the scenes.

Unlike the more opportunistic, fire-and-forget campaigns we've observed from some other DPRK actors, `TraderTraitor` seems to favor a big-game hunting approach, carefully selecting high-value targets and investing considerable effort in post-compromise operations.

For me, that's what makes this group particularly interesting. Even after years of tracking DPRK threat actors, I still find something surprising whenever I take a closer look at this group's operations.

RT @willdepue: I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at https://t.co/YOtzND0Jqk.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.
